target.title: feat(feishu): bot-to-bot conversation support with @mention handling
target.body:
## Summary

Makes Feishu bot-to-bot conversations actually work. Bot-authored messages already reach dispatch on `main` (nothing gates them out), so bots could already "talk" — but the experience was broken: replies frequently never reached the peer bot because the `@mention` was missing or used the wrong syntax for the payload, so the conversation silently died. This PR makes bot-to-bot replies reliable — correct, payload-aware `@mention` delivery on every visible path (text, chunked, card, streaming) — and adds opt-in (`allowBots`) plus loop-protection controls. (In a Feishu group a message only notifies the entities it explicitly `@mentions`, so a reply without the right `@` is silently never delivered.)

- Continue treating incoming bot messages like user messages (now gated by an `allowBots` opt-in) so the agent can take part in bot-to-bot threads.
- New `bot-name` resolution module backed by the bot batch API as a weak dependency: falls back to the `open_id` when the bot info scope is absent.
- Per-chat mention registry resolving display name → `open_id` for outbound use.
- Outbound mention handling: teach `<at user_id="...">` syntax in the system prompt, strip only the leading self-mention, preserve + dedup other mentions, escape `<`/`>` in display names.
- Guarantee bot-to-bot replies `@mention` the bot sender via a deterministic `ensureMention` backstop, applied **per outbound unit** (every text chunk and the streaming-card close) using the **syntax that matches the payload** — `<at user_id="...">` for text/post messages, `<at id=...>` for lark_md cards — so the peer bot is notified on every visible path. Replies are delivered inline, not in a topic thread.
- `allowBots` opt-in (default: accept, preserving current behavior) lets operators set `false` to ignore bots or `"mentions"` to accept only when `@mentioned`.
- Shared bot-pair loop guard: bot-authored turns are wired into core `botLoopProtection` (sliding window, on by default) plus a Layer-1 self-filter that drops the bot's own webhook echoes.
- Core owns the group reply-delivery mode; the feishu `@mention` hint stays delivery-mode-agnostic (no duplicate delivery-mode computation in the plugin).

Aligns with #71396 — main no longer auto-prepends mentions, so this does not reintroduce the third-party mention cascade: the `mentionTargets` block stays context-only and never tells the model to re-`@` listed users.

Scope: changes are under `extensions/feishu/**` plus the feishu docs page. The one non-plugin file is `src/config/bundled-channel-config-metadata.generated.ts`, regenerated (`pnpm config:channels:gen`) because the new `allowBots`/`botLoopProtection` config fields must appear in the aggregated bundled-plugin config metadata that the config-metadata check validates.

## Verification

- `pnpm test extensions/feishu` — green, including the new/updated `outbound-mention`, `reply-dispatcher`, `bot` (bot-authored handling), and `monitor` suites covering card vs text mention syntax, per-chunk mentions, `allowBots` gating, and loop-guard suppression.
- `pnpm config:channels:gen --check`, `tsgo`, and `oxlint` clean for the touched surface.
- Real-machine verification in a live Feishu group (see proof below).

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: a group bot-to-bot reply now `@mentions` the bot sender so the other bot actually receives it — across text messages, chunked replies, and lark_md cards; replies to a human still `@` the human; a silent turn stays `NO_REPLY`. With `allowBots: false` the bot ignores other bots' messages. Previously a bot replying to a bot could omit the `@` (or use the wrong card syntax) and the reply was silently never delivered.

Real environment tested: a live Feishu group containing two bots and one human participant; the agent ran as one bot and replied across multiple turns to the other bot and to the human, under both text and card render modes, and with `allowBots` toggled. (Identifiers below are redacted.)

Exact steps or command run after this patch: ran `pnpm config:channels:gen`, rebuilt and restarted the gateway, then drove a multi-turn bot-to-bot exchange in the live group; captured the agent session trajectory and compared it against the messages actually delivered to the group; toggled `allowBots` and a tight `botLoopProtection` window to observe gating.

Evidence after fix:

- On turns where the sender was the other bot, the inbound prompt carried `[System: "<name>" (open_id: ou_<bot-sender-redacted>) is a bot and receives your reply only if you @mention it. You MUST @mention it in your reply.]`, and the reply led with the bot sender's `<at>` — the peer bot received it.
- `ensureMention` backstop verified live: on a turn where the raw model output omitted the bot sender's `@`, the message actually delivered to the group still contained it — the dispatcher backfilled it.
- Card path verified live: a reply rendered as a lark_md card carried the card mention syntax (`<at id=...>`) and the peer bot received it (the text-form tag would not have notified inside a card).
- `allowBots` verified live: with `allowBots` disabled, the peer bot's messages no longer triggered a reply.

Copied live output from the session (open_ids and names redacted):

```text
# Inbound prompt to the agent — sender is the other bot:
[System: "<bot>" (open_id: ou_REDACTED) is a bot and receives your reply only if
 you @mention it. You MUST @mention it in your reply.]

# Agent reply that turn, as delivered to the group — leads with the bot sender's <at>:
<at user_id="ou_REDACTED"><bot></at> 好，背景比较清晰，… (reply continues)

# A later turn whose raw model output dropped the bot-sender @ (it only @'d the
# human). The message ACTUALLY delivered to the group still carried it — the
# dispatcher's ensureMention backfilled the bot sender before sending:
<at user_id="ou_REDACTED"><bot></at> <at user_id="ou_REDACTED_HUMAN"><human></at> 面试结论：…
```

Observed result after fix: the other bot received and continued the conversation across turns under both text and card modes; no silent drop. `allowBots: false` cleanly suppressed bot-authored replies. Replies addressed exactly the intended target and stayed inline.

What was not tested: the `message_tool` visible-reply path does not receive the deterministic backstop by design (see Design notes); that is an intentional product decision, not an untested gap.

## Design notes

- **Per-payload mention syntax.** Feishu uses two `<at>` forms: `<at user_id="...">Name</at>` for text/post messages and `<at id=...></at>` for lark_md cards. The backstop emits the form matching each outbound unit and re-applies it per chunk and on streaming-card close, so a long or card-rendered bot-to-bot reply notifies the peer on every message.
- **The deterministic backstop is intentionally scoped to the `automatic` reply path, not `message_tool`.** `automatic` is an implicit reply where the agent does not directly control delivery, so the dispatcher guarantees the bot-sender `@`. The `message_tool` path (`messages.groupChat.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`) is an explicit, flexible send where the agent deliberately authors the message, recipients, and mentions; the plugin respects what the agent wrote and does **not** auto-inject — forcing one would override an intentional, author-controlled send. Outbound mention normalization still runs on both paths, so any `@` the agent does write is resolved correctly.
- **Bot-pair loop protection.** Bot-authored messages already reached dispatch on `main` (no gate drops them), so the bot-pair possibility is not introduced here. This PR adds the safety: `allowBots` (default accept; `false`/`"mentions"` to restrict), a Layer-1 self-filter that drops the bot's own webhook echoes, and wiring of accepted bot-authored turns into core's shared `botLoopProtection` sliding-window guard (on by default). Tunable/disable-able via `channels.feishu.botLoopProtection`.

target.title: fix(browser): stop agent-launched managed Chrome
target.body:
Closes #109678

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running `openclaw browser stop` after an agent launched managed Chrome could still see `running: true` while the Chrome process and CDP listener remained alive.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stop transition now recovers a local managed Chrome that was launched by another browser runtime, while staying inside the profile lifecycle transition so later starts cannot race ahead of cleanup. It closes only a process proven to match the current-host singleton lock, configured executable, exact CDP port and user-data-dir arguments, process start identity, and listening socket; attach-only and remote profiles remain disconnect-only.

## User Impact

`openclaw browser stop` can now stop the same managed Chrome regardless of whether the CLI/Gateway process or an agent-side browser runtime retained the original launch handle. External and remote browsers are not terminated.

## Evidence

- Regression-first proof on current main: the two new cases failed because the cross-runtime stop helper was absent and `stopRunningBrowser()` returned `stopped: false`.
- Focused browser lifecycle suite: 5 files passed, 108 tests passed via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`.
- Targeted `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` passed for all four changed files.
- Fresh pre-commit autoreview reported no accepted/actionable findings.
- Full `check:changed` was not run locally: Blacksmith Testbox was unavailable because this machine is not authenticated to the `openclaw` organization.
- Initial pull request checks: Real behavior proof, Security Sensitive Guard, Auto response, Dependency Guard detection, and ClawSweeper dispatch passed. Labeler failed while GitHub refused its repository-content request with `fail-fast:network`; Dependency Guard enforcement and one security detection checkout were cancelled before code execution by the same trusted-base checkout/network problem. Fork contributors cannot rerun these admin-owned workflows.

### Real macOS behavior proof

Ran the built `openclaw.mjs` from commit `7ec1917` against Google Chrome on macOS with an isolated state directory and redacted ephemeral Gateway credentials. A separate agent-runtime process launched the managed profile and retained its launch handle; the Gateway and `openclaw browser stop` ran in different processes.

```text
REAL_MACOS_PROOF OpenClaw=2026.7.2 commit=7ec1917
AGENT_MANAGED_BEFORE pid=20009 cdp=60698 process=ALIVE listener=LISTEN
CLI_STOP_MANAGED exit=0 profile=managed-proof running=false cdpReady=false
AGENT_MANAGED_AFTER pid=20009 process=EXITED cdp=60698 listener=CLOSED

CLI_STOP_ATTACH_ONLY exit=0 profile=attach-proof running=true cdpReady=true
ATTACH_ONLY_AFTER pid=20165 process=ALIVE cdp=60699 listener=LISTEN
PROOF_RESULT PASS tokens=REDACTED state=ISOLATED
```

The attach-only Chrome was terminated explicitly only during proof cleanup.

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

target.title: fix(infra): import legacy plugin state partially (newest-first) instead of skipping when capacity is short
target.body:
Fixes a regression from #108744 ([`13a52cf0a53`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/13a52cf0a53)): the startup preflight made legacy plugin-state imports all-or-nothing, so whenever the target namespace (or the 50k per-plugin cap) couldn't fit **every** missing legacy entry, the whole import was skipped. The Telegram sent-message cache migration targets the same namespace the live cache writes to (cap 10,000), so on busy installs the namespace stays near-full and the migration was a **permanent no-op** retried on every startup until legacy entries aged past the TTL. A mid-import cap eviction additionally rolled back the entire import and retry-looped across startups.

Requested by obviyus in the Discord #maintainers "Telegram Migration" thread: startup/upgrade must never be blocked, and the migration must not permanently no-op.

### What changed

- **Partial, newest-first imports.** The preflight computes an import budget of `min(namespace remaining, per-plugin remaining)` and imports the newest entries that fit instead of skipping everything. Plan entries carry an optional `timestamp` (epoch ms; falls back to remaining `ttlMs`, which is monotone with recency for fixed-TTL caches). The Telegram sent-message lister now provides it.
- **Eviction tolerance instead of whole-import rollback.** If a concurrent write causes a cap eviction mid-import, only the entry whose write triggered the eviction is rolled back; an evicted pre-existing live row is restored when its value is still known; everything imported so far stays. The run pauses and defers the remainder.
- **Deferred remainder imports later.** The legacy source stays in place while any entries are deferred, so later startups import the rest as capacity frees. Archival of fully-covered sources and the `cleanupWhenEmpty` behavior for fully-expired files are unchanged, as is the intentional TTL-boundary drop.
- **Consistent capacity math.** The preflight now uses the effective per-plugin cap (`resolveMaxPluginStateEntriesPerPlugin`) so its math matches actual store enforcement.
- Log messages now report partial progress, e.g. `Partially migrating … importing the newest X and deferring the rest in the legacy source` and `Paused migrating … imported X of Y missing entries`.

### Tests

New/updated unit tests in `doctor-state-migrations.test.ts`: newest-first partial import under a namespace cap, deferred remainder importing on a later run once capacity frees, zero-capacity deferral without blocking startup, per-plugin-cap partial import, and mid-import eviction tolerance (concurrent writes simulated by seeding sibling entries after the preflight count).

<details>
<summary>Evidence / verification</summary>

- Regression source: #108744, commit [`13a52cf0a53`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/13a52cf0a53); skip site was `src/infra/state-migrations.plugin-state.ts` (`Skipped migrating … has room for X of Y missing entries`), rollback site was the `cap evicted` path in the same file.
- Telegram sent-message cache: `TELEGRAM_SENT_MESSAGE_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = 10_000`, live cache and migration share `telegram.sent-messages`, 24h TTL — a busy install keeps the namespace full, so `missing > remaining` held indefinitely.
- `pnpm vitest run src/commands/doctor-state-migrations.test.ts` → 89 passed
- `pnpm vitest run src/plugin-state/` → 64 passed
- `pnpm vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-telegram.config.ts extensions/telegram/src/state-migrations.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/send.test.ts` → 182 passed
- `pnpm tsgo:all` clean; `oxlint` / `oxfmt --check` clean on changed files

</details>

target.title: fix(discord): bound gateway metadata response reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed and understand the change.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `fetchDiscordGatewayInfo` could buffer an unbounded response body via `response.text()` when fetching the Discord `/gateway/bot` metadata endpoint.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Streaming pre-read bound (primary path):** When the response body stream is available, the function now uses `readResponseWithLimit` to enforce the 4 MiB cap **before** buffering — the stream is read in chunks and cancelled on overflow, matching the existing `materializeGuardedResponse` pattern used by `fetchDiscordGatewayMetadataGuarded`.

**Post-hoc fallback (body-less path):** When the body stream is unavailable (rare polyfill or mock edge case), the function falls back to `text()` with a byte-length check after buffering. This preserves backward compatibility with `DiscordGatewayFetch` implementations that return body-less mock responses.

**Non-transient overflow:** Size overflow now throws as non-transient (`transient: false`) so the detail message propagates to callers instead of being swallowed by the generic "fetch failed" wrapper.

## User Impact

Discord Gateway connections now reject oversized/hostile metadata responses **before** buffering the full body into memory. Normal responses (a few KB of JSON) are completely unaffected. The `DiscordGatewayFetch` type contract is backward-compatible — callers that don't provide `body` continue to work via the post-hoc fallback.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/monitor/gateway-metadata.test.ts --run`: **8/8 passed**.
- `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check` passed.
- The test coverage includes: body-less success, body-less oversized rejection, **real loopback HTTP streaming oversized rejection** (pre-read bound verified), and a load-bearing mutation test.

target.title: feat(skills): preview proposals before approval
target.body:
Closes #103871

## Summary

- add a read-only `review` action to `skill_workshop`
- render create proposals as the complete canonical skill that would be applied and update proposals as unified diffs
- bound previews with line-aware pagination, proposal-version binding, and explicit drift/integrity outcomes
- keep presentation portable so channels can attach “View skill” / “View diff” actions without owning Skill Workshop policy

## Problem

Approval messages currently provide only a prose summary. Operators cannot inspect the exact skill that a create proposal will install or see additions and removals in an update before approving it.

## Design and safety

The review projection lives beside Skill Workshop validation and apply semantics. The service computes one canonical read-only result; the agent tool owns bounded presentation and pagination; channels only render portable actions.

An approval prompt describes a specific proposal snapshot, so its execution is deliberately bound to the resolved proposal ID and current version. This is fail-closed: if a proposal changes while the operator is reviewing it, the old approval cannot apply the newer content. A code-site invariant now documents this coupling. Direct service, CLI, and tool calls remain Proposal-ID-only compatible because `proposal_version` is still optional outside the approval gate.

## User impact

- create proposals can be reviewed in full before approval
- update proposals show an exact unified diff
- Approve and Reject remain available on every preview page, including page 1
- stale approval prompts fail with expected/current version feedback
- existing direct Proposal-ID lifecycle calls remain compatible

## Evidence

- 239 focused Vitest tests pass on final head `d5c1be51d406858d447fa97658ca72bdb1ad8872`.
- Production and test tsgo checks pass.

target.title: fix(models): clear stale auth cooldowns after early limit resets
target.body:
Related: #70903

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who resolve a provider usage or billing condition before its recorded reset time can remain stuck on fallback because the saved auth profile is still locally blocked.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a profile-scoped `openclaw models auth clear-cooldown <profile-id>` command that reuses the existing locked reset operation, targets the persisted owner of inherited profiles, verifies the authoritative stored result, and prints the safe-restart step needed to discard live Gateway bookkeeping. It deliberately does not add polling, shorten provider backoffs, change fallback policy, restart services implicitly, or remove credentials.

## User Impact

Operators can safely re-evaluate a recovered provider without editing SQLite or repeating OAuth. If the underlying failure still applies, the next request can restore the cooldown normally.

target.title: refactor(channels): centralize inbound orchestration and remove internal compat
target.body:
Closes #109316

## What Problem This Solves

Internal and bundled message channels still assembled core-owned route, session, context, history, retry, dispatch, and delivery behavior through deprecated low-level compatibility surfaces. That duplicated lifecycle logic across transports and allowed public Plugin SDK compatibility APIs to become internal architecture.

## Why This Change Was Made

Core now owns normalized inbound turn planning and dispatch: route/envelope construction, direct-DM access, session conflict retry, history/media handling, session recording, durable delivery, feedback reflection, and lifecycle ordering. Bundled channels provide transport facts and native send/reaction/typing operations only. Internal callers use focused modern seams; shipped compatibility remains only at public SDK, released input/data, doctor/migration, or external dependency boundaries.

The stack is intentionally one PR but split into subsystem commits: core turn kernel, runtime compat removal, architecture guards, memory, Teams feedback, bundled channel migrations, direct-DM/envelope cleanup, tests, and generated SDK baseline.

## User Impact

No intended user-visible behavior change. Plugin authors keep shipped compatibility during its existing deprecation window. Maintainers get one core-owned inbound lifecycle, transport-thinner channels, and hard guards against new internal deprecated-facade use.

Non-test TypeScript using the task's `*.test.ts` exclusion: **+2525 / -2542, net -17 lines**.

target.title: fix(docker): bound smoke installer curl with connect timeout
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed and understand the change.

## What Problem This Solves

The install-sh-smoke Docker runner executes a direct `curl | bash` one-liner with no overall pipeline timeout. While `run_installer_for_package_spec` and the freshness path use `timeout(1)` to bound the complete pipeline, this direct invocation had no process-level deadline — a hung post-download installer could consume the harness's full container timeout.

## Why This Change Was Made

Wrap the entire `curl | bash` pipeline in `timeout --kill-after=30s "${INSTALL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT}s"`, **matching the existing `run_installer_for_package_spec` pattern exactly**. The curl-level `--connect-timeout 30` and `--max-time 300` flags are retained as defence-in-depth — the process-level timeout bounds the complete pipeline (download + install), while the curl-level timeouts fail fast on network stalls without waiting for the full `INSTALL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT` (default 900 s).

The fix is at `scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh:338-340` where the direct installer one-liner is changed from a bare `curl | bash` to a `timeout`-wrapped equivalent.

## User Impact

Smoke test CI jobs now fail within the configured `INSTALL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT` when either the download or the subsequent installation hangs. The freshness smoke and `run_installer_for_package_spec` paths already had this protection; now all three installer pipelines are consistently bounded.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts --run -t "runs candidate tarballs"`: passed.
- `bash -n scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh`: passed (no syntax errors).
- The guard test verifies both the `timeout --kill-after=30s` wrapper and the `--connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300` flags.
- Rebased onto current `origin/main` (no conflicts).

### Real behavior proof (timeout pipeline bounded termination)

```
$ sed -n '337,340p' scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh
echo "==> Run official installer one-liner"
timeout --kill-after=30s "${INSTALL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT}s"   bash -c 'curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300 "$1" | bash -s -- --no-prompt'   _ "$INSTALL_URL"

# Healthy pipeline completes within timeout:
$ timeout --kill-after=2s 5s bash -c 'echo ok'; echo $?
ok
0  (success)

# Hung pipeline terminated by timeout:
$ timeout --kill-after=2s 3s bash -c 'sleep 999'; echo $?
124  (timeout killed the command, elapsed ~3s)
```

The `timeout` wrapper kills the entire pipeline (curl + bash) after `INSTALL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT` seconds, with a 30 s grace period for SIGKILL. This matches the existing pattern used by `run_installer_for_package_spec` exactly.

target.title: fix(cron): skip deleteAfterRun and preserve counters for manual runs (#83538)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw cron run` (a manual/operator run) on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot ("at") job used to delete the job on success — consuming the one-shot so its scheduled fire never happened (issue #83538). Manual runs also mutated `consecutiveErrors` / `consecutiveSkipped` counters and `nextRunAtMs`, corrupting the scheduled retry/backoff/next-run state that only real scheduler executions should own.

The root cause is that `applyJobResult()` had no notion of *who* triggered a run: manual, scheduled (timer), and the gateway on-exit watcher all shared one finalization path, so `shouldDelete` and the counter mutations fired for every successful run regardless of origin.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix threads an explicit `CronRunOrigin` (`"timer" | "watcher-terminal" | "operator"`) through cron finalization. `applyJobResult` derives `consumesOneShot` and `ownsSchedulerState` as `origin !== "operator"` and records `lastRunWasManual = origin === "operator"`, so operator runs record the outcome only (never consume a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot, never touch scheduler counters / `nextRunAtMs` / enabled state), while `timer` and `watcher-terminal` runs keep consuming and owning scheduler state — preserving the merged on-exit `deleteAfterRun` contract from #104550.

`origin` is kept strictly internal. It is **not** part of the public `CronServiceRunOptions`: exposing it there would let any in-process facade caller (plugin SDK, RPC handlers, tests) request `watcher-terminal` semantics and delete one-shots or mutate scheduler-owned counters/backoff/timing. Instead, the public `run` is always operator semantics, and the gateway on-exit watcher — the only legitimate non-operator caller, which already holds the concrete `CronService` instance — uses a concrete-only `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` entry (absent from `CronServiceContract` / `GatewayCronServiceContract`) to get consuming behavior. The invalid-persisted-run path (`skipInvalidPersistedManualRun`) also forwards the true caller origin instead of hard-coding `operator`, so an invalid watcher-terminal run keeps scheduler-owned semantics.

## User Impact

- Debugging/manually running a scheduled `deleteAfterRun` job no longer silently cancels its upcoming scheduled fire.
- Manual runs no longer corrupt retry backoff, auto-disable, or next-run timing of scheduled jobs.
- Gateway on-exit watcher-terminal one-shots continue to be consumed exactly as before (no regression for the #104550 contract).
- The scheduler-consuming origin is no longer reachable through the public cron API, so plugins/RPC/tests cannot accidentally (or intentionally) delete one-shots or mutate scheduler state via `run`.

## Evidence

Real-setup proof at the current head using a **real running OpenClaw gateway process and the real `openclaw cron` CLI** (not a vitest/function harness). Built from this head and run inside a `node:24-bookworm` container (container node v24.18.0; the repo engines floor is 24.15.0), against a real on-disk cron store (sqlite).

```
Head: c071ce7ca34e7a41e4fafab4a8863960fb9403c7
Gateway: OpenClaw 2026.7.2 (c071ce7)   dist/build-info.json commit = c071ce7c...

Built-artifact fix verification (fix compiled into the running gateway):
  dist/server-cron-*.js contains:
    async runOnExitTerminal(id, payload) { ... }
    run: (jobId, payload) => cron.runOnExitTerminal(jobId, payload)
  'watcher-terminal' occurs only inside runOnExitTerminal; the public run path
  forwards no origin.

PART A — OPERATOR PRESERVATION (real `openclaw cron run`)
  $ openclaw cron add "partA-ok-preserve" --at "+2h" --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
    -> id 3c309f88..., nextRunAtMs 1784045230759
  $ openclaw cron run 3c309f88... --wait
    -> {"status":"ok", exitCode 0}          (operator path, success)
  $ openclaw cron get 3c309f88...
    -> job STILL PRESENT, enabled:true, deleteAfterRun:true,
       nextRunAtMs 1784045230759 (UNCHANGED), lastRunWasManual:true,
       no consecutiveErrors / no backoff mutation
  => successful operator run did NOT consume the one-shot, scheduler state intact.

PART B — WATCHER-TERMINAL CONSUMPTION (real gateway on-exit watcher cycle)
  $ openclaw cron add "partB-onexit-consume" --on-exit "sleep 8; echo ..." \
        --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
  # real gateway watcher armed + spawned the watched process (seen in ps):
  #   bash -lc sleep 8   /   sleep 8
  [cron] cron-exit: watcher armed { jobId: a27c2044... }
  [cron] cron-exit: watched command exited; firing job { exitCode: 0 }
  $ openclaw cron get a27c2044...      -> "cron job not found"
  $ openclaw cron list                 -> only the 2 PART A jobs remain
  $ sqlite3 .../openclaw.sqlite 'select job_id from cron_jobs'  -> 2 rows (no partB)
  => real on-exit watcher-terminal run DID consume/delete the successful one-shot.

OVERALL: PASS — driven end-to-end through a live gateway + operator CLI + real
on-disk store. Operator and watcher-terminal origins are cleanly separated, and
the scheduler-consuming origin is unreachable from the public cron API.
```

Unit/regression coverage at head: the public `CronServiceContract.run` preserves a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot (operator semantics, no scheduler-state mutation) even though it can no longer request another origin, `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` still consumes a successful on-exit one-shot, and invalid watcher-terminal runs keep scheduler-owned semantics while operator invalid runs stay operator-attributed.

Persisted-state coverage for `lastRunWasManual` (`timer.backoff-config-readback.test.ts`, real on-disk sqlite store): a **fresh store** where a manual/operator error run persists `lastRunWasManual: true`, reloads from sqlite, and keeps the natural next-run slot (no backoff floor, `consecutiveErrors` untouched) so the scheduled fire still triggers on a fresh service state; and an **upgraded store** whose persisted job predates the field (no `lastRunWasManual` on disk) — on reload the absent field is treated as a scheduled run, so the error backoff window still applies and the past-due slot is correctly suppressed. This proves the new optional field degrades safely for both new and pre-existing stores.

### Proof equivalence: transcript head → current head

The live-setup transcript above was captured at `c071ce7c`. The branch head has since been rebased onto newer `main` (current head `c42041b0`). Scoped to the cron runtime surface exercised by the transcript (`src/cron/service/`, `src/gateway/server-cron.ts`), the full non-test delta between `c071ce7c` and the current head is:

- **`export`-keyword removals on now-module-local symbols** — `onTimer`, `executeJobCore` (`timer.ts`); `resetActiveCronTaskRunsForTests`, `CRON_TASK_RUN_SETTLEMENT_TRACKING_MAX_MS` (`active-run-cancellation.ts`); `DEFAULT_JOB_TIMEOUT_MS`, `AGENT_TURN_SAFETY_TIMEOUT_MS` (`timeout-policy.ts`). Values and in-module usage unchanged; no prod file outside each defining module imported them.
- **test-support extraction** — `timer.ts` and `active-run-cancellation.ts` now expose those test-only helpers via a `globalThis` symbol registered inside an `if (process.env.VITEST || process.env.NODE_ENV === "test")` guard, imported by new `*.test-support.ts` modules. This block is a no-op in a production gateway.
- **four appended `/* oxlint-disable max-lines */` directive comments** (`jobs.ts`, `ops.ts`, `timer.ts`, `server-cron.ts`).
- **rebased-in `main` change #104430 ("cap trigger script tool access")** — `mergeCronPayload` and its `toolsAllow` helpers moved out of `jobs.ts` into the new `src/cron/service/payload-merge.ts`, with cross-payload-kind `toolsAllow` marker handling. This is genuine upstream behavior on the `cron.update` payload-merge / trigger-script tool-access surface, disjoint from scheduler counters and one-shot consumption; it arrived through the rebase and is not part of this PR's proof scope.
- **`server-cron.ts` `toolsAllow` type-guard simplification** — the trigger-script call now reads `job.payload.toolsAllow` directly (valid once #104430 lifted `toolsAllow` to a shared `CronPayload` field) instead of gating on `kind === "agentTurn"`. This is on the trigger-script tool-access path, not the `runOnExitTerminal` / delete-after-run wiring.

None of these touch the delete-after-run / origin / backoff / one-shot-consumption / scheduler-state control flow. The `CronRunOrigin` threading, `consumesOneShot` / `ownsSchedulerState` (`origin !== "operator"`), `lastRunWasManual` (`origin === "operator"`), `shouldDelete = wouldDelete && consumesOneShot` in `timer.ts`, the `ops.ts` origin forwarding, and the `runOnExitTerminal` wiring in `server-cron.ts` are unchanged. The recorded operator-preservation and watcher-terminal-consumption behavior therefore holds on the current head. Reviewers can confirm the delta with:

```

```

target.title: fix(feishu): lock timeoutMs preflight abort for stalled DNS lookup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Feishu app registration goes through `fetchWithSsrFGuard`. Operators need a locked regression that a **stalled DNS/proxy preflight** is cancelled by the guard's existing top-level `timeoutMs` before any HTTP request is dispatched.

## Why This Change Was Made

ClawSweeper P1 on the prior tip identified that the `signal: AbortSignal.timeout()` path in `fetchFeishuJson` drops guard-owned timeout diagnostics. This iteration restores `timeoutMs` (the guard's top-level param), keeping the shared `request timed out` diagnostic and `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` preflight abort.

**This iteration:**
- Rebased on latest `main`
- **Kept** guard `timeoutMs` (no production ownership change)
- Added stalled-lookup regression next to the existing hang-POST timeout proof, matching its outcome shape

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where agent runs repeatedly issuing the same blocked tool call could never reach the configured global circuit breaker after critical loop blocking began. Critical tool-loop vetoes were excluded from no-progress accounting, freezing the streak below the higher global threshold.

target.title: fix(tlon): bound Urbit auth response body drain to prevent OOM
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed and understand the change.

## What Problem This Solves

The Urbit login flow in the Tlon extension reads the entire response body via `response.text()` solely to flush the stream so that `set-cookie` headers finalize. The body content is discarded. This call had no size bound — a misconfigured or hostile Urbit endpoint could stream gigabytes into process memory during login.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace the unbounded `response.text()` body drain with a **streaming reader with a 64 KiB cumulative drain budget**. When the body stream is available (Node 18+, Bun, Deno), the reader accumulates chunks in a bounded loop until the total drained bytes reach the threshold, then the reader is cancelled in a `finally` block so it is released even when `read()` throws. The 64 KiB value is an **accounting threshold** — `reader.read()` returns producer-defined chunks, so a single chunk may push the running total above 64 KiB before the threshold is detected on the next iteration check. This prevents unbounded accumulation.

**No unbounded fallback:** When no body stream is available, there is no body to drain — cookie headers are already finalised. The previous `response.text()` fallback was removed entirely so both code paths are bounded.

## User Impact

Urbit login no longer risks OOM from an oversized response body. Normal login flows (small JSON responses) are completely unaffected. The cookie extraction behavior is unchanged — the `set-cookie` header is available as soon as the stream is cancelled or consumed.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/tlon/src/urbit/auth.ssrf.test.ts --run`: **5/5 passed**.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- Three drain tests cover: streamed body drain with cookie extraction, oversized stream cancellation after 64 KiB threshold, and body-less responses (skip drain, cookie extracted).

### Real behavior proof (loopback HTTP with production authenticate())

Two loopback HTTP servers, exercising the real production `authenticate()` function:

```json
{"case":"real-loopback-small-body","cookie":"urbauth-~zod=proof-token-789; Path=/; HttpOnly","result":"cookie_extracted_successfully"}
{"case":"real-loopback-oversized-body","cookie":"urbauth-~zod=oversized-drain; Path=/; HttpOnly","result":"cookie_extracted_after_bounded_drain"}
```

- **Small body:** Normal login succeeds, cookie extracted.
- **Oversized body (256 KiB > 64 KiB drain cap):** Bounded drain, stream cancelled, cookie STILL extracted.

The proof uses the full production path: `authenticate()` → `urbitFetch()` → SSRF guard → streaming drain → cookie header access. Real `node:http` servers, no stubs.

target.title: fix(ai): bound openai-chatgpt-responses WebSocket with handshakeTimeout and maxPayload
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: The `connectWebSocket` function in `openai-chatgpt-responses` creates a WebSocket connection without any handshake timeout or message size limit. If the server accepts TCP but never completes the WebSocket upgrade, the connection hangs indefinitely. Oversized messages could also cause OOM.

**Solution**: Implement transport-neutral bounds using the existing lifecycle cleanup path rather than `ws`-specific constructor options:
- **Handshake timeout**: `setTimeout`-based 30s deadline that calls `socket.close()` and rejects the promise. Wrapped in try-catch so a throwing `close()` never leaves the promise unsettled. Works across Node, Bun, and browser globals.
- **Message size limit**: Byte-accurate enforcement in `decodeWebSocketData` using `TextEncoder` or raw `ArrayBuffer.byteLength` before materializing the JS string. Correctly bounds multibyte UTF-8 payloads unlike a simple `text.length` check.
- **Regression tests**: Stalled-handshake timeout, oversized message rejection (ASCII and multibyte), and throwing-close resilience.

**What changed**: Two files — source code and tests. ~120 lines net.

**What did NOT change**: No API changes, no `ws`-specific constructor options, no changes to `getWebSocketConstructor()`, `acquireWebSocket()`, or the SSE fallback path.

Fixes #109566

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Unbounded WebSocket handshake wait and oversized message OOM risk

**Real environment tested**: Node.js v24.13.1 / Linux / ws library / net module controlled server

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
npx tsx evidence-collect.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
━━ Test 1: Stalled WebSocket handshake → timeout ━━
  [server] TCP listening on 127.0.0.1:28760
  [server] TCP accepted, holding without upgrade...
  [server] received 377 bytes (WS upgrade request), ignoring
  ✅ connectWebSocket rejected after 5034ms
  ✅ Error: WebSocket connection handshake timed out
  ✅ Timeout accuracy: PASS (expected ~5000ms, got 5034ms)

━━ Test 2: Oversized message → close code 1009 ━━
  [server] WS server listening on 127.0.0.1:28761
  [server] WebSocket upgrade complete
  [client] Sending oversized message (17.0 MiB)
  ✅ Oversized message rejected with CodexProtocolError
  ✅ Error: WebSocket message exceeds maximum size of 16777216 bytes
  ✅ Close code 1009 (Message Too Big) was sent to peer

━━ Test 3: Byte accuracy — multibyte UTF-8 payload ━━
  Character: € (U+20AC) — 3 UTF-8 bytes, 1 UTF-16 code unit
  UTF-16 length (text.length, BEFORE fix): 5941932 chars  (UNDER limit)
  UTF-8  length (TextEncoder, AFTER fix):  17825796 bytes (OVER limit)
  ✅ Byte-accurate check correctly catches multibyte payloads
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All three bounds are verified with real controlled-server evidence. Handshake timeout correctly fires at ~5s with the expected error message. Oversized messages are rejected with close code 1009. Multibyte UTF-8 payloads that would pass a naive `text.length` check are correctly caught by the byte-accurate enforcement.

**What was not tested**: No real OpenAI API call. Evidence uses controlled local TCP/WS servers. SSE fallback path (unchanged) not tested.

---

## Tests and validation

4 regression tests:
1. Stalled handshake timeout — connectWebSocketForTest rejects after deadline
2. Oversized ASCII message — parseWebSocket rejects > 16 MiB payload
3. Multibyte oversized message — non-ASCII payload correctly bounded by byte count
4. Throwing-close resilience — socket.close() throwing during handshake timeout does not prevent promise settlement

## Risk checklist

- [x] Backwards compatible — no API changes
- [x] Transport-neutral — works on Node, Bun, browser globals
- [x] Byte-accurate — correct for multibyte UTF-8 payloads
- [x] Throwing-close guard — promise always settled
- [x] merge-risk: low — ~120 lines net, regression tests + real evidence

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Follow-up to #109332, attacking the two ~250s serial CI bins that now own main-run wall time, plus a profiled 130s module-evaluation stall:

1. **`src/plugin-sdk/anthropic-cli.ts` stalled ~131s per cold worker on CI.** It snapshots `CLAUDE_CLI_BACKEND_ID` at module scope through the sync facade loader, which on source checkouts jiti-evaluates the anthropic plugin's **full `api.js` barrel** (Testbox import profile: `anthropic-cli.ts` self-time 130.86s). Every graph that reaches `src/agents/cli-runner/prepare.ts` paid it — this is why `agentic-agents-core-runner-cli` stripes ran 157–245s for two files whose tests finish in 1s, and why yesterday's timing census concluded the file "cannot be split further".
2. **`core-fast` (268s) and `core-tooling` (265s) ran as single jobs on the full/main plan.** core-fast is import-bound (247s vitest: 181s module evaluation vs 49s tests); core-tooling is test-time bound (173s of spawned-process tests). The compact PR plan already stripes tooling; the full plan did not.

## Why This Change Was Made

Maintainer-requested bundled follow-up ("do all of it, one larger PR"). After #109332 and the caching waves (#109330/#109425/#109593), these were the measured critical-path items.

## User Impact

- CI main-run wall time: the two ~265s bins become ~5 jobs of ~60–110s each; the cli stripes drop from a 245s tail to ordinary ~15s bins.
- Contributors on source checkouts stop paying a silent 130s jiti stall in any test whose graph touches `cli-runner/prepare.ts`.
- Compact PR plans gain the docker tooling helper coverage they previously dropped (the docker config now rides with the isolated shard on both plans), and the compact-only tooling expansion is deleted (one striping path).

## Evidence

- **Testbox proof of the stall fix**: `vitest.agents-core` on `cli-runner.reliability + helpers`: **157.6s → 14.25s** (import 155.7s → 12.8s); import profile before/after names `src/plugin-sdk/anthropic-cli.ts` (130.86s self) as the sole whale. New narrow artifact `extensions/anthropic/cli-api.ts` follows the documented lightweight-artifact pattern (`extensions/CLAUDE.md`), knip models it like the browser artifacts, and `pnpm plugin-sdk:surface:check` is clean (facade exports unchanged).
- **Full-plan striping**: `core-unit-fast` → 2 include-list stripes (8 vCPU, admission wave 0, stripe 1 is the vitest fs-cache writer) + a whole `core-unit-fast-isolated` shard (isolated + fake-timer projects stay unsliced); `core-tooling` → 4 stripes + combined docker+isolated shard, shared by full and compact plans. Planner invariants tested: stripes partition files with no overlap, bundled include coverage equals base coverage, cache-warm workflow warms the union of unit-fast configs.
- **Hints**: rebased onto the fresh 5-run census (#109717) and corrected only the entries the stall fix invalidates (cli stripes 245/18/8 → 15/15/8, with the measured Testbox rationale in the comment).
- Tests: `ci-node-test-plan`, `ci-workflow-guards`, `ci-changed-node-test-plan`, `ci-run-node-test-shard`, `plugin-sdk-subpaths` contract, `extensions/anthropic/cli-shared`, `cli-runner/prepare` — all green post-rebase (300+ assertions). Remote `pnpm build` green (facade/lazy-boundary rule). Codex autoreview (gpt-5.6-sol, xhigh): clean.
- Not addressed here (measured, needs its own session): `check-prompt-snapshots` stays ~196s — still ~304s on a 16 vCPU Testbox **with** the facade fix, so its cost is broad graph execution under tsx, not the stall.

target.title: fix(agents): preserve thinking default precedence for listed agents
target.body:
<!-- submission-timestamps:start -->
First submitted: July 17, 2026, 12:05 AM (US Eastern Time) / 04:05 UTC.
Last body edit: July 17, 2026, 2:09 AM (US Eastern Time) / 06:09 UTC.
Latest head commit: July 17, 2026, 1:37 AM (US Eastern Time) / 05:37 UTC.
<!-- submission-timestamps:end -->

Closes #109276

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an inconsistency where `resolveAgentConfig()` returned only an explicit
`agents.list[].thinkingDefault` value even though its contract says that agent
defaults have already been applied. Callers that inspect the resolved config
could therefore observe `undefined` for a listed agent while the effective
runtime later inherited `agents.defaults.thinkingDefault` through another
resolution path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The direct nullish fallback suggested by the issue is incomplete on its own.
Several runtime callers intentionally treat the value from the agent entry as
an explicit override before evaluating per-model `params.thinking`, the global
default, and provider/model defaults. Returning the merged global value through
those override-sensitive paths would make the global default incorrectly win
over a per-model setting.

This change separates the two contracts:

- `resolveAgentConfig()` now returns the documented merged value.
- `resolveAgentThinkingDefaultOverride()` returns only the explicit per-agent
  value for precedence-sensitive runtime paths.

The command, reply model-selection, subagent inheritance, gateway session, and
startup-summary paths use the explicit helper where provenance matters.

## User Impact

Consumers of `resolveAgentConfig()` can now rely on a listed agent inheriting
`agents.defaults.thinkingDefault`. Existing runtime precedence remains intact:

1. session or message override
2. explicit per-agent default
3. per-model `params.thinking`
4. global `agents.defaults.thinkingDefault`
5. provider/model default

Explicit `off` values remain authoritative because the merge uses nullish, not
truthy, fallback semantics.

## Breaking Changes

None expected. This restores the documented merged-config contract while
preserving the existing runtime precedence order.

## Implementation

- Add `resolveAgentThinkingDefaultOverride()` at the agent-scope owner boundary.
- Merge `thinkingDefault` in `resolveAgentConfig()` with agent-over-global
  nullish precedence.
- Route precedence-sensitive callers through the explicit override helper.
- Add focused tests for merged inheritance, explicit `off`, and a listed agent
  whose per-model thinking setting must still outrank the global default.

## Code-Path Analysis

- Owner: `src/agents/agent-scope-config.ts`
- Public facade: `src/agents/agent-scope.ts`
- Runtime callers: `src/auto-reply/reply/model-selection.ts`,
  `src/agents/command/model-selection.ts`, `src/agents/subagent-spawn.ts`,
  `src/gateway/session-utils.ts`, `src/gateway/server-startup-log.ts`
- Adjacent precedence owner: `src/agents/model-thinking-default.ts`
- Tests: `src/agents/agent-scope.test.ts`,
  `src/auto-reply/reply/model-selection.test.ts`, plus existing command,
  subagent, gateway-session, and startup-summary coverage
- Contract: `src/config/types.agents.ts` and `docs/tools/thinking.md`

## Mainline Comparison

- Official base: `OpenClaw/OpenClaw:main@399345e1bb1b472969cf586bd1400536e940a3cc`
- Base fetched/verified: July 17, 2026, 05:37 UTC
- Current main still returned only `entry.thinkingDefault` from the merged
  resolver. Recent same-surface changes did not implement this provenance split.

## Branch/Base Provenance

- Base: `OpenClaw/OpenClaw:main@399345e1bb1b472969cf586bd1400536e940a3cc`
- Head: `snowzlmbot/OpenClaw:fix/109276-thinking-default-fallback@c58a6f981f64167e33806c0bf936121d13db704b`
- The head branch was created/replayed directly from the official base.
- The fork default branch was not used as the implementation baseline and was
  not modified by this work.

## Dependency/Contract Verification

No external dependency contract changed. The configuration type already states
that `agents.list[].thinkingDefault` overrides
`agents.defaults.thinkingDefault`, and the thinking documentation already
defines per-model thinking ahead of the global default. The implementation now
preserves both contracts explicitly.

## Labels Considered

- `agents`
- `P2`
- `impact:auth-provider`
- `merge-risk: compatibility` because configuration-default precedence is
  compatibility-sensitive

These are suggestions only; this contribution does not claim maintainer label
authority.

## Validation

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/agent-scope.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/model-selection.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/agent.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/agent-command.live-model-switch.test.ts`
- focused gateway session/startup and subagent tests selected by changed-file CI
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs -- src/agents/agent-scope-config.ts src/agents/agent-scope.ts src/agents/agent-scope.test.ts src/agents/agent-command.live-model-switch.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/model-selection.ts src/auto-reply/reply/model-selection.test.ts src/agents/command/model-selection.ts src/agents/subagent-spawn.ts src/gateway/session-utils.ts src/gateway/server-startup-log.ts`
- `git diff --check`

## Evidence Source Map

- Successful exact-head downstream CI: [evidence workflow run](https://github.com/snowzlmbot/openclaw/actions/runs/29557157953)
  - Tested head: `7592d0e708c7814dc2d1d37bc2487f6a1ff38628`
  - Tested base: `44b79d44ae1353fcd90159605453b43ec190b6e1`

  - Passed `check-lint`, agent command, reply/model-selection, subagent, gateway, plugin SDK, Control UI i18n, type/check, and `openclaw/ci-gate` lanes.

  - Current head `c58a6f981f64167e33806c0bf936121d13db704b` is a patch-identical rebase onto `399345e1bb1b472969cf586bd1400536e940a3cc`.
  - Stable patch id before and after rebase: `56c224c2908f0adc231d6126d6454fe5926b45a3`.

  - Tested base: `19b5e564d7e363a6249e1704f3363eff81395305`

- Earlier patch run: [comparison workflow run](https://github.com/snowzlmbot/openclaw/actions/runs/29555662547)
  - Confirmed contribution-owned format, lint, type, agent command, model-selection, subagent, and gateway lanes passed; an unrelated timing-sensitive plugin SDK assertion was isolated before the final all-green run.

## Sanitized Logs

```text

Precedence guard: listed agent without override + per-model thinking + global default -> per-model value

```

No credentials, hostnames, internal paths, account identifiers, or private
runtime data are included.

## Media Evidence

This is a non-visual configuration-resolution change. The linked Actions run
provides the complete reproducible source-level flow and exact-head result;
there is no UI state or dynamic interaction for a screenshot or recording to
clarify.

## Risk

- Compatibility: callers that intentionally inspect merged config now observe
  the documented global fallback.
- Precedence: mitigated by keeping explicit agent provenance in a dedicated
  helper and by regression coverage for per-model-over-global behavior.
- Performance: one normalized agent-entry lookup replaces an equivalent config
  lookup at the affected callers; no new I/O or runtime catalog loading.
- Security/privacy: no authorization, secret, persistence, or transport changes.

Revert this PR. No schema migration, persisted-data rewrite, config migration,
or irreversible operation is introduced.

No documentation change is required. `docs/tools/thinking.md` and the config
type comments already describe the precedence restored by this implementation.

- Closes #109276
- Historical same-area fixes: #86689 and #63418

target.title: fix(infra): import legacy plugin state partially (newest-first) instead of skipping when capacity is short
target.body:
Fixes a regression from #108744 ([`13a52cf0a53`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/13a52cf0a53)): the startup preflight made legacy plugin-state imports all-or-nothing, so whenever the target namespace (or the 50k per-plugin cap) couldn't fit **every** missing legacy entry, the whole import was skipped. The Telegram sent-message cache migration targets the same namespace the live cache writes to (cap 10,000), so on busy installs the namespace stays near-full and the migration was a **permanent no-op** retried on every startup until legacy entries aged past the TTL. A mid-import cap eviction additionally rolled back the entire import and retry-looped across startups.

Requested by obviyus in the Discord #maintainers "Telegram Migration" thread: startup/upgrade must never be blocked, and the migration must not permanently no-op.

### What changed

- **Partial, newest-first imports.** The preflight computes an import budget of `min(namespace remaining, per-plugin remaining)` and imports the newest entries that fit instead of skipping everything. Plan entries carry an optional `timestamp` (epoch ms; falls back to remaining `ttlMs`, which is monotone with recency for fixed-TTL caches). The Telegram sent-message lister now provides it.
- **Eviction tolerance instead of whole-import rollback.** If a concurrent write causes a cap eviction mid-import, only the entry whose write triggered the eviction is rolled back; an evicted pre-existing live row is restored when its value is still known; everything imported so far stays. The run pauses and defers the remainder.
- **Deferred remainder imports later.** The legacy source stays in place while any entries are deferred, so later startups import the rest as capacity frees. Archival of fully-covered sources and the `cleanupWhenEmpty` behavior for fully-expired files are unchanged, as is the intentional TTL-boundary drop.
- **Consistent capacity math.** The preflight now uses the effective per-plugin cap (`resolveMaxPluginStateEntriesPerPlugin`) so its math matches actual store enforcement.
- Log messages now report partial progress, e.g. `Partially migrating … importing the newest X and deferring the rest in the legacy source` and `Paused migrating … imported X of Y missing entries`.

### Tests

New/updated unit tests in `doctor-state-migrations.test.ts`: newest-first partial import under a namespace cap, deferred remainder importing on a later run once capacity frees, zero-capacity deferral without blocking startup, per-plugin-cap partial import, and mid-import eviction tolerance (concurrent writes simulated by seeding sibling entries after the preflight count).

<details>
<summary>Evidence / verification</summary>

- Regression source: #108744, commit [`13a52cf0a53`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/13a52cf0a53); skip site was `src/infra/state-migrations.plugin-state.ts` (`Skipped migrating … has room for X of Y missing entries`), rollback site was the `cap evicted` path in the same file.
- Telegram sent-message cache: `TELEGRAM_SENT_MESSAGE_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = 10_000`, live cache and migration share `telegram.sent-messages`, 24h TTL — a busy install keeps the namespace full, so `missing > remaining` held indefinitely.
- `pnpm vitest run src/commands/doctor-state-migrations.test.ts` → 89 passed
- `pnpm vitest run src/plugin-state/` → 64 passed
- `pnpm vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-telegram.config.ts extensions/telegram/src/state-migrations.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/send.test.ts` → 182 passed
- `pnpm tsgo:all` clean; `oxlint` / `oxfmt --check` clean on changed files

</details>

target.title: fix(auto-reply): deliverBindingPayload missing abortSignal check
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugin binding notifications could still be delivered via `routeReplyToOriginating`, `dispatcher.sendToolResult`, or `dispatcher.sendFinalReply` after the dispatch operation has been aborted, because `deliverBindingPayload` did not check or propagate the dispatch abort signal. The same gap existed in the fast-abort acknowledgment path: it propagated `abortSignal` but lacked a post-route guard before the direct-dispatcher fallback.

## Why This Change Was Made

`deliverBindingPayload` was missing the same abort-signal guard that `sendPayloadAsync` (the sibling function) already implements. Aligned them by adding:

1. **Pre-check**: `getDispatchAbortSignal()` + `.aborted` early return
2. **Propagation**: pass `abortSignal` to `routeReplyToOriginating` options
3. **Post-check**: after the async `routeReplyToOriginating` call, check `.aborted` again before falling through to `sendToolResult`/`sendFinalReply`

The fast-abort acknowledgment path had the same pattern: it propagated `abortSignal` through `routeReplyToOriginating` but did not re-check after the await, so a cancellation during routed delivery could still reach `dispatcher.sendFinalReply` on the wrong surface.

Since all callers of `deliverBindingPayload` are in the same closure that already has `getDispatchAbortSignal()`, no parameter changes were needed.

## User Impact

Users of plugin bindings may see fewer stale/misdirected binding notifications when a dispatch operation is aborted (e.g. session timeout, manual cancellation). The fast-abort acknowledgment is similarly guarded against wrong-surface delivery after cancellation. No behavior change for normal (non-aborted) dispatch paths.

## Evidence

### Test results

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.acp-abort.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.reply-dispatch.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.lifecycle-and-bindings.test-utils.ts

 ✓ 3 files  →  311 tests passed (311)
```

### Lint and type checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `tsgo:core` (type) | ✅ |
| `test-types` | ✅ |
| `oxlint` | ✅ |
| `oxfmt` | ✅ |

### Mid-route abort regression (deliverBindingPayload post-check)

Abort fires synchronously inside `routeReply` mock, simulating the race window:

```
[C] 1. AbortController created (signal.aborted = false)
[C] 2. routeReply mock invoked — firing abortController.abort()
[C] 5. Calling dispatchReplyFromConfig with abortSignal...
[C] 6. Result: {"queuedFinal":false,"counts":{"tool":0,"block":0,"final":0}}
[C] 8. sendFinalReply NOT called:  ✓ (post-check guard active)
[C] 🎯 VERDICT: Binding reply was SUPPRESSED (no delivery)
```

### E2E QA gateway proof (pre-aborted signal)

Real QA bus server + real `handleQaInbound` + real `dispatchReplyWithBufferedBlockDispatcher`:

```
 ✓ |extension-qa| proof-109109-abort-gateway.test.ts (1 test)

[E2E] QA bus started: http://127.0.0.1:42989
[E2E] abortSignal:    aborted = true
[E2E] ✅ routeReply NOT called (short-circuited at entry guard)
[E2E] ✅ Binding reply SUPPRESSED
```

### Fast-abort post-route guard

After the `routeReplyToOriginating` await returns null, `getDispatchAbortSignal()?.aborted` is checked before the `dispatcher.sendFinalReply` fallback, preventing wrong-surface delivery when cancellation races with the route.

## Files changed

| File | ± | Change |
|------|---|--------|
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.ts` | +19/−1 | deliverBindingPayload pre/post abort checks + signal propagation; fastAbort path signal propagation + post-route guard |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.lifecycle-and-bindings.test-utils.ts` | +98 | Regression test: mid-route abort race window in plugin binding delivery |
| `extensions/qa-channel/src/inbound.ts` | +3 | Optional `abortSignal` parameter on `handleQaInbound`, forwarded into dispatch `replyOptions` |

target.title: fix(qa-lab-web): guard dashboard json responses

## What Problem This Solves
Fixes an issue where the QA Lab web dashboard would throw raw JSON parse errors when an API route returned a non-JSON or empty success body.

## Why This Change Was Made
The dashboard HTTP helper now treats JSON as an explicit contract: it rejects non-JSON success bodies and empty bodies with a clear route-labeled error instead of letting `response.json()` fail unpredictably. Error responses stay readable through the same helper.

The follow-up on this head removes the earlier global 64 KiB success-body cap so valid large dashboard payloads, including the production `/api/state` polling payload, are not rejected by the client helper.

## User Impact
Dashboard actions now fail with a stable, labeled error when the backend returns malformed or unexpected JSON, while valid large JSON responses can still be consumed by polling/rendering paths.

## What Problem This Solves

`streamAnthropic` (in `packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.ts`) builds `output.errorMessage` in its catch block from the bare error message. For an SDK HTTP error this collapses to a status-only string like "529 status code (no body)" and drops the response body that carries the real failure reason, so Anthropic 429/overloaded/5xx failures are hard to diagnose from the surfaced error.

PR #109556 introduced `formatProviderError` and applied it to `google-shared.ts` and `openai-completions.ts` to surface HTTP status + body as "<status>: <body>". The anthropic provider's catch block is the same shape but was missed in that pass. This adopts the helper there so Anthropic matches the other OpenAI-compatible providers; non-HTTP errors keep their existing message via the helper's fallback path.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(infra): gateway pid probe no longer hangs when ps sampling stalls
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readGatewayProcessArgsSync` (in `src/infra/gateway-processes.ts`) probes `ps` on darwin to read a gateway process's argv **before** signaling it or reporting it as a verified listener PID. The darwin branch already passed a 1000ms timeout, but {BT}spawnSync{BT} defaults `killSignal` to SIGTERM, which an unresponsive or hung `ps` child can ignore. As a result a stalled `ps` probe can keep the gateway process blocked past the configured timeout, hanging gateway signal verification and listener PID discovery.

This is the same class of stall already fixed for the doctor TUI process probe in #109243, applied to the gateway's own pid-verification path.

## Evidence

- The fix adds `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to the `spawnSync("ps", ...)` call so a stalled probe is reaped at the deadline instead of hanging, and extracts the timeout into a named `GATEWAY_PS_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS` constant.
- Local vitest run of `src/infra/gateway-processes.test.ts` is green: 8 passed (8), including the darwin path.
- The darwin test now asserts the full `spawnSync` options shape - encoding, killSignal, timeout - locking in the behavior (mirrors the assertion added in #109243).

```ts
const ps = spawnSync("ps", ["-o", "command=", "-p", String(pid)], {
  encoding: "utf8",
  killSignal: "SIGKILL",
  timeout: GATEWAY_PS_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS,
});
```

target.title: fix(compaction): count CJK text in token estimates
target.body:
Closes #103930

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where CJK-heavy sessions retain far more recent conversation than `keepRecentTokens` intends after compaction. The cut-point estimator treated CJK text as four characters per token, so Chinese, Japanese, and Korean content could be retained at roughly three to four times the configured token budget.

## Why This Change Was Made

The compaction estimator now uses the repository's existing CJK-aware character accounting for every textual message shape. That helper now lives in `@openclaw/normalization-core`, which both the root runtime and standalone `agent-core` can import without duplicating Unicode-range behavior; the existing root module remains a compatibility re-export.

## User Impact

CJK-heavy conversations now compact to approximately the same retained-token budget as equivalent ASCII conversations. ASCII estimates and image accounting are unchanged.

## Evidence

Before: the unmodified production estimator returned 40 estimated tokens for 160 CJK characters—the same result as 160 ASCII characters—and selected cut point index 1 for four such messages with a 100-token budget.

After, driving the real exported production functions on this branch:

```console
$ node --import tsx --input-type=module …
{"cjkTokens":160,"extensionBTokens":160,"cutPoint":3}
```

target.title: fix(microsoft-foundry): keep spawn pipe streams UTF-8 safe across chunk splits
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Azure CLI login output captured from child_process spawn could show corrupted multibyte text (for example CJK or emoji) in terminal output and error messages when a UTF-8 code point was split across stdout/stderr chunk boundaries (`String(chunk)` per Buffer → U+FFFD).

Related prior art: #108518 (`provider-local-service` `setEncoding("utf8")`) and #109220 (`voice-call` ngrok tunnel logs).

## Why This Change Was Made

`azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions` pipes now decode stdout/stderr statefully with `setEncoding("utf8")` before line buffering and output forwarding.

## User Impact

Operators running Azure CLI login through the Microsoft Foundry extension see intact Unicode in terminal output and error-derived messages instead of `�` when output is chunked mid-character.

## Evidence

### Changes

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/microsoft-foundry/cli.ts` | +8/−4 — add `setEncoding("utf8")` before stdout/stderr data handlers |
| `extensions/microsoft-foundry/index.test.ts` | +73/−24 — mock regression test calling `azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions` + real-spawn integration test |
| `scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs` | +79/−0 — standalone proof script anyone can run to verify before/after behavior |

### Tests

```
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  95 passed (95)
```

### Proof

**1. Production-function regression test (mock spawn)**

Calls `azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions({})` through a controlled `spawn()` mock that returns a fake ChildProcess with `PassThrough` streams. Writes a 4-byte UTF-8 smiley (U+1F60A) split across two `stderr` writes at the exact byte boundary where raw `Buffer.toString()` would produce U+FFFD, then emits `close(1)`. Asserts the rejection error contains the cleanly reassembled `😊` — proving the production function's `setEncoding` + error-output path work correctly together.

**2. Real-spawn integration test**

Uses `vi.importActual` to bypass the module mock and get the real `spawn` from `node:child_process`. Spawns a real Node.js child (`process.execPath -e ...`) that writes `Buffer.from([0xf0, 0x9f, 0x98, 0x8a])` split across two `process.stdout.write` calls with a 10 ms delay — simulating real pipe chunking that Azure CLI would produce. Applies the same `setEncoding("utf8")` that the production fix uses, collects data chunks, and asserts the output is the clean `😊` without U+FFFD. This proves the stateful decoder mechanism works with real OS pipes and real child process I/O.

**3. Standalone proof script (`scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs`)**

Anyone can run `node scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs` to verify the before/after behavior on their own machine. Terminal output:

```
❌ WITHOUT setEncoding (old behaviour)
    per-chunk hex:              f09f  988a
    per-chunk String():          "�" + "��"
    joined result:              "���"
    has U+FFFD (�):              true

✅ WITH setEncoding (fix)
    per-chunk strings:           "😊"
    joined result:              "😊"
    has U+FFFD (�):              false
```

**4. Real spawned `az` end-to-end proof (see PR comment)**

Creates a fake `az` executable on an isolated PATH that writes a 4-byte UTF-8 smiley split across two `stderr` writes 50 ms apart, then spawns `az login --use-device-code` with and without `setEncoding("utf8")`. This exercises the exact same `spawn("az", ["login", "--use-device-code"], ...)` path as the production function, through a real OS pipe buffer. See the PR comment for live terminal output.

Combined proof coverage:

| Layer | What it proves | Method |
|-------|---------------|--------|
| Production function logic | `azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions` handles setEncoding → data → accumulation → close → error correctly | Mock `spawn()` with `PassThrough` streams |
| Real OS pipe decoder | `setEncoding("utf8")` reassembles split bytes on real spawned pipes | Fake `az` on PATH, real `spawn()` with same args as production function |
| Reproducibility | Any operator can verify before/after on their machine | Standalone `scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs` |

### Non-goals / boundaries

- Does not add Azure CLI binary dependency to tests.
- Does not change `execAz` (uses `execFileSync` with `encoding: "utf-8"`) or `execAzAsync` (uses SDK `runExec` wrapper) — both already handle encoding correctly.
